name: AI and Online Banking Safety
objectives: Using your phone or computer, open your bank's official app or website from the app store or the address on your statement, never through a link in a text or email
When you sign in to online banking, use a long, unique password and two-step verification, and sign out on shared computers, sharing your password and codes with no one
In your bank's app or website, turn on alerts for large purchases, low balance and sign-in changes, with at least two alerts on
Given a call or message that says it is your bank, identify the signs of a fake bank contact and call the number on the back of your card, without giving a code, password or money
Before sending money with a payment app, check the person's name and number and send only to people you know in person, never paying someone who contacted you first
If money or information is stolen, call your bank, change your password and report it to the right places, starting right away with the number on your card

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Getting your bank's real app or website
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find and open your bank's official app or website without being tricked by a fake.
This lesson builds toward: Using your phone or computer, you will open your bank's official app or website from the app store or the address on your statement, never through a link in a text or email.
Scammers make fake bank apps and websites that look real. AI makes the copies look even better. So start from a source you trust.
For the app: open the official app store on your phone, search your bank's exact name, and check that the app is published by your bank. If you are unsure, your bank's official website or a branch employee can tell you the app's exact name. For the website: type your bank's address yourself, or use the address printed on your statement. Do not reach your bank through a link in a text or email.
Your bank can also help you set up online banking at a branch or by phone, using the number on the back of your card.
Step by step:
- Open the official app store.
- Search your bank's exact name.
- Check that the app is published by your bank.
- On a computer, type the address from your statement yourself.
- Never use a link in a text or email to reach your bank.
Words to know:
- Online banking: using your bank's app or website to see and manage your accounts.
- Fake app: an app made to look like a real one in order to steal information.
Try it now: Look at a bank statement or your bank card and find your bank's website address and phone number. Write them on a card you keep at home.
You can now find your bank's real app or website from a trusted source.

check.q: Where is your bank's real website address printed?
options: In a text from an unknown number
In an email asking you to update details
check.why: Type the address from your statement yourself instead of using a link.

check.q: You find two apps with your bank's name in the app store. What do you check?
options: Which one is published by your bank
Which one has the brightest logo
check.why: Check that the app is published by your bank; ask your bank if you are unsure.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Signing in safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Sign in with a strong password and two-step verification, and sign out safely.
This lesson builds toward: When you sign in to online banking, you will use a long, unique password and two-step verification, and sign out on shared computers, sharing your password and codes with no one.
Your password should be long and hard to guess: a phrase of several unrelated words works well. Use it only for your bank. Keep it in a safe place at home or in a password manager, never in a plain note on your phone, and never share it.
Two-step verification (also called two-factor) adds a second check, usually a code texted to your phone or a prompt in the app. Even if someone learns your password, they cannot get in without that code. Turn it on in the app's security settings, or ask your bank to help.
Your bank will never call or text to ask you for that code. Anyone who asks for it is a scammer. Many apps also let you sign in with your fingerprint or face, which is safe and easy. On a shared or library computer, do not save your password, and sign out when done.
Step by step:
- Choose a long, unique password, such as several unrelated words.
- Keep it somewhere safe, never in a plain note.
- Turn on two-step verification.
- Never share the code with anyone.
- Sign out on shared computers.
Words to know:
- Two-step verification: a second check, such as a texted code, needed to sign in.
- Password manager: an app that safely stores your passwords.
Try it now: With a family member or bank employee if you like, open your bank's app or website and check that two-step verification is turned on. If not, turn it on. Do not share any codes with anyone, including us.
You can now sign in safely with a strong password and two-step verification.

options: A second check, such as a texted code, after your password
check.why: It adds a second check, so a password alone is not enough to get in.

check.q: You need a new bank password. Which is best?
options: The same password you use for email
A phrase of several unrelated words, used only for your bank
check.why: A long, unique phrase of unrelated words is strong and hard to guess.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Setting up alerts to catch problems early
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn on account alerts so you notice unusual activity quickly.
This lesson builds toward: In your bank's app or website, you will turn on alerts for large purchases, low balance and sign-in changes, with at least two alerts on.
Alerts are messages your bank sends you by text, email or app notification when something happens in your account: a large purchase, a low balance, a new payee or a password change.
In the bank's app or website, look for Alerts or Notifications, often under your profile or settings. Turn on alerts for purchases over an amount you choose, low balance, and any change to your sign-in details.
When an alert arrives for something you did not do, do not reply to it or call a number in it. Open your bank's app yourself, or call the number on the back of your card.
Step by step:
- Open your bank's app or website.
- Find Alerts or Notifications.
- Turn on alerts for large purchases, low balance and sign-in changes.
- If an alert shows something you did not do, call the number on your card.
Words to know:
- Alert: a message from your bank about activity in your account.
- Payee: a person or company you send money to.
Try it now: Turn on at least two alerts in your bank's app or website: one for purchases over an amount you choose, and one for a low balance.
You can now set up bank alerts and respond safely when one arrives.

options: A message from your bank when something happens in your account
A call from the fraud department
check.why: Alerts tell you about activity such as a large purchase or a low balance.

check.q: An alert says you changed your password, but you did not. What do you do?
options: Call the number in the alert
Open your bank's app yourself or call the number on your card
check.why: Do not reply or call a number in the alert; reach your bank yourself.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Spotting scams and staying protected

lessons.title: Lesson 4: AI-powered fake bank calls and messages
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Recognize a fake "bank fraud department" call or message.
This lesson builds toward: Given a call or message that says it is your bank, you will identify the signs of a fake bank contact and call the number on the back of your card, without giving a code, password or money.
A common scam: a call or text says it is your bank's fraud department and there is a problem with your account. The caller ID may even show your bank's name, and AI can make the voice and messages sound very professional.
Then they ask you to do something: read them a code, "verify" your password, move your money to a "safe account", withdraw cash for a courier, or buy gift cards. These are the FTC's scam signs: pretending, a problem, pressure, and an unusual way to pay. The FTC says real organizations will never tell you to move money to protect it.
What to do: hang up. Then call the number on the back of your card yourself. If it was real, the bank will know about it.
Step by step:
- Notice: a "bank" contacts you about a problem.
- Notice: they ask for a code, password, money move, cash or gift cards.
- Hang up or stop replying.
- Call the number on the back of your card yourself.
Words to know:
- Spoofing: making a fake caller ID show a real company's name or number.
- Safe account scam: a trick telling you to move your money to "protect" it, straight to the scammer.
Official sources:
- FTC: How to avoid a scam
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant: "What are signs that a call from my bank's fraud department is fake?" Compare its answer with this lesson, and write the three you think are most important on your card.
You can now recognize a fake bank call or message and check it safely.

check.q: What does it mean when a caller's ID shows your bank's name?
options: Nothing for sure; caller ID can be faked
You must call back the same number
check.why: Scammers can make caller ID show your bank's name.

check.q: A "fraud department" caller says to move your savings to a safe account today. What do you do?
options: Give them your password to check
Hang up and call the number on the back of your card
check.why: Real organizations never tell you to move money to protect it; hang up and call your bank yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Using payment apps carefully
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Send money with a payment app only to people you know and trust.
This lesson builds toward: Before sending money with a payment app, you will check the person's name and number and send only to people you know in person, never paying someone who contacted you first.
Payment apps (such as Zelle, Venmo, PayPal and Cash App) let you send money from your phone. They are handy for paying back a family member, but the money usually moves instantly and can be very hard to get back.
Only send money to people you know in person. Double-check the name, phone number or email before you send. Never pay a stranger, an online seller you do not know, or anyone who contacted you first claiming to be your bank, the government or a company.
Be careful of "accidental payment" tricks: a stranger sends you money and asks you to send it back. Do not send it; contact your bank or the app company through its official app or website.
Step by step:
- Only pay people you know in person.
- Double-check the name and number before sending.
- Never pay someone who contacted you first.
- If a stranger "accidentally" pays you, contact your bank or the app, do not send money back.
Words to know:
- Payment app: an app that sends money from your phone to another person.
- Instant transfer: money that moves right away and is hard to reverse.
Official sources:
- FTC: How to avoid a scam (payment red flags)
Try it now: Write on your card: "I only use payment apps with people I know in person. I never pay anyone who contacts me first."
You can now use payment apps safely and avoid common payment app tricks.

check.q: Why be careful with payment apps?
options: Money usually moves instantly and is hard to get back
check.why: Payment app money moves fast and is very hard to recover.

check.q: You want to pay back your niece $20 by app. What do you do before you tap Send?
options: Double-check her name and phone number
Send it to the first name that appears
Ask a stranger to send it
check.why: Double-checking the name and number stops money going to the wrong person.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: If something goes wrong
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the steps to take quickly if money or information is stolen.
This lesson builds toward: If money or information is stolen, you will call your bank, change your password and report it to the right places, starting right away with the number on your card.
Act fast. Call your bank right away using the number on the back of your card. Tell them what happened. Ask them to stop or reverse payments if possible, change your password, and watch your account.
Then report it. Report the scam to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If someone is using your identity, go to IdentityTheft.gov for a free recovery plan. If you are 60 or older, the National Elder Fraud Hotline is free: 833-FRAUD-11 (833-372-8311).
Watch for a second scam: people who call offering to "recover" your money for a fee are usually scammers too. And there is no shame in being targeted. Telling a trusted family member helps protect you and others.
Step by step:
- Call your bank on the number on your card right away.
- Change your password.
- Report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
- Use IdentityTheft.gov if your identity was used.
- Age 60+: call 833-372-8311.
- Ignore anyone offering to recover money for a fee.
Words to know:
- Identity theft: when someone uses your personal information to pretend to be you.
- Recovery scam: a trick where scammers offer to get back stolen money for a fee.
Official sources:
- FTC: Report fraud
- FTC: What to know about identity theft
- DOJ Office for Victims of Crime: National Elder Fraud Hotline
Try it now: Final task: sign in to your bank's official app or website, turn on two alerts, write your bank's number from the back of your card on your safety card, and judge this sample text with the four signs: "BANK ALERT: Your account is locked. Verify now at the link or it will be closed today."
You can now bank online safely, spot fake bank contacts, use payment apps carefully, and act quickly if something goes wrong.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Official app or website Signed in through a link in a message or an unofficial app. Signed in through the official app from the app store or the address typed from the statement. Can show how to check that the app is published by the bank. Safe sign-in Password is short, reused or written in a plain phone note. Signed in with a strong password and two-step verification turned on. Uses fingerprint or face sign-in, or a password manager, and knows the bank never asks for the code. Alerts on Fewer than two alerts turned on. At least two alerts on, such as large purchases and low balance. Also turned on alerts for sign-in or password changes. Bank number on the safety card No number, or a number copied from a message. The bank's number from the back of the card is written on the safety card. Also lists ReportFraud.ftc.gov and, if 60 or older, the Elder Fraud Hotline. Sample text judged Missed that the sample "bank" text was a scam. Judged the sample text correctly and named the signs found. Said exactly what to do next: do not reply, call the number on the card. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: A free recovery plan if someone uses your identity
check.why: IdentityTheft.gov gives a free recovery plan.

check.q: You just realized you sent money to a scammer. What is your first step?
options: Call your bank right away on the number on your card
Pay a company to recover it
check.why: Act fast: call your bank first, then report the scam.
